tagline: Cradle of democracy and the Olympics
overview:
Greece occupies the southern tip of the Balkan Peninsula, where the land shatters into thousands of islands scattered across the blue Aegean and Ionian Seas. It is about the size of Alabama, but no country in Europe has a longer coastline compared with its size. The capital, Athens, is one of the oldest cities in the world, its ancient Acropolis hill crowned by the Parthenon temple, standing above a sprawling modern city of about three million people.

Around 10.4 million people live in Greece and speak Greek, a language with its own alphabet that has been written for nearly 3,000 years. Most Greeks belong to the Orthodox Christian Church. Greece is a parliamentary republic and a member of the European Union, and it uses the euro. Shipping, tourism, olives, and farming drive the economy; Greek shipowners control one of the largest merchant fleets in the world. Ancient Greeks gave the world democracy, philosophy, theater, and the Olympic Games, and modern Greeks live among those ruins with a love of sunshine, sea, and long meals shared with family.
landAndNature: About 80 percent of Greece is mountains. The Pindus range forms the country's spine, and Mount Olympus, the mythical home of the gods, is the highest peak at 2,917 meters. The Vikos Gorge in the north is one of the deepest canyons in the world. Around 6,000 islands and islets, of which about 200 are inhabited, dot the seas: Crete is the largest, and the Cyclades are famous for whitewashed villages and blue-domed churches. Meteora's monasteries perch atop sandstone pillars hundreds of meters high. Summers are hot and dry, winters mild on the coast and snowy in the mountains. Loggerhead turtles nest on Zakynthos, rare monk seals hide in island caves, and wild goats called kri-kri live on Crete, while olive trees, some over a thousand years old, cover the hills.
peopleAndCulture: Greek life centers on family, food, and the outdoors. Meals feature olive oil, feta cheese, olives, grilled fish, souvlaki, moussaka, and honey-soaked baklava, often at tavernas late into the evening. Coffee is sipped slowly, and dancing in a line with arms on shoulders breaks out at weddings and festivals. Easter is the biggest holiday, with candlelit midnight services and roasted lamb. Greeks celebrate name days as much as birthdays. Soccer and basketball are the top sports; Greece won the European soccer championship in 2004 in a huge upset. Theater, born here 2,500 years ago, is still performed in ancient stone amphitheaters under the stars, and the bouzouki, a long-necked string instrument, gives Greek music its distinctive sound.
history: The Minoans of Crete built palaces by 2000 BC, followed by the Mycenaeans of Homer's epics. Around 500 BC, city-states like Athens and Sparta flourished; Athens created the world's first democracy, and thinkers such as Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle laid the foundations of Western philosophy and science. Alexander the Great spread Greek culture as far as India before Rome absorbed Greece in 146 BC. The Byzantine Empire, Greek-speaking and Christian, ruled from Constantinople for a thousand years until the Ottomans conquered it in 1453 and ruled Greece for nearly four centuries. Greeks won independence in a war beginning in 1821. Greece was occupied by Nazi Germany in World War II, suffered a civil war, and endured a military dictatorship from 1967 to 1974 before restoring democracy. It joined the European Union in 1981.
funFacts: The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896, reviving a tradition that began in Olympia in 776 BC.
Greece has about 6,000 islands and islets, and about 200 of them have people living on them year-round.
The marathon race is named after the town of Marathon, from which a messenger supposedly ran to Athens in 490 BC.
Greeks are among the top consumers of olive oil in the world, using more than 12 liters per person each year.
Greece has 18 UNESCO World Heritage Sites, including the Acropolis, Delphi, and the monasteries of Meteora.
